author: HSinghHira
tagline: End-to-end encrypted photo storage on SeaweedFS object storage
description:
Ente is a self-hosted, end-to-end encrypted platform to store, share, and rediscover your photos and videos across all your devices. This build stores them in SeaweedFS, an actively maintained open-source object store built for very large numbers of files.

**Features**

- End-to-end encryption for every photo and video you upload.

- Web app for your library plus a separate public-albums app for
  sharing.


- SeaweedFS all-in-one server for S3-compatible object storage — one
  container running master, volume server, filer and S3 gateway.


- Fast reads even with millions of files, which suits a large photo
  library.


- SeaweedFS credentials and Ente's buckets are created automatically
  on first start.


- PostgreSQL 17 for accounts, albums and photo metadata.

- Bundled Mailpit catcher for sign-up verification codes — no SMTP
  setup required to get started, with the option to switch to a real
  provider later.


- Persistent storage under /DATA/AppData/$AppID for PostgreSQL and
  SeaweedFS data.


**How to use?**
1. Open Ente Photos (SeaweedFS) from the Zima OS dashboard.
2. Sign up for an account in the web app.
3. Open Mailpit at http://your-nas-ip:8461 and read the verification
   code.

4. Type the code into the web app to finish signing up.
5. Every new account starts with Ente's normal 10 GB limit. Raise it
   with a one-time database command — see the install tips.

6. Start uploading photos and videos, and set up a public album to
   share with others.

7. SMTP settings and the S3 address can be changed later in the
   service environment variables — no rebuild needed, just a
   container restart.

tips.before_install:
1. Find your Zima OS box's IP address. You will need it three times.
2. Open the app settings before you install.
3. In the museum service, replace CHANGEME_NAS_IP in
   ENTE_S3_B2_EU_CEN_ENDPOINT with that IP.

4. In the museum service, replace CHANGEME_NAS_IP in
   ENTE_APPS_PUBLIC_ALBUMS with that IP.

5. In the web service, replace CHANGEME_NAS_IP in ENTE_API_ORIGIN
   with that IP.

6. Do not use localhost. Phones cannot reach it.
7. Pick a new database password. Make one at randomkeygen.com.
8. Put it in ENTE_DB_PASSWORD (museum) and POSTGRES_PASSWORD
   (postgres). Both must match.

9. Pick a new storage password. Make one at randomkeygen.com.
10. Put it in ENTE_S3_B2_EU_CEN_SECRET (museum), S3_SECRET_KEY
    (seaweedfs-config) and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (seaweedfs-init).
    All three must match.

11. Replace ENTE_KEY_ENCRYPTION, ENTE_KEY_HASH and ENTE_JWT_SECRET
    in the museum service with your own values from
    randomkeygen.com.

12. Start the Ente Photos (SeaweedFS) installation.
13. Wait for the enteseaweedfs-init container to finish before you
    sign up. It creates the buckets.

14. Open Ente Photos (SeaweedFS) from the Zima OS dashboard.
15. Sign up, then read your code at http://your-nas-ip:8461.
16. Your account starts with a 10 GB limit. To raise it, run:
    docker exec enteseaweedfs-postgres psql -U pguser -d ente_db -c
    "UPDATE subscriptions SET storage = 109951162777600;"

17. That command sets every account on this server to about
    100 TB. Run it again any time you add a new account.

18. Important: the s3.json file is written once. If you change the
    keys later, delete
    /DATA/AppData/enteseaweedfs/seaweedfs_config/s3.json and
    restart.

19. Important: changing a password later does not change it inside
    PostgreSQL. Set it before the first start.

20. Important: changing ENTE_KEY_ENCRYPTION after you upload
    photos makes those photos unreadable.

title: Ente Photos (SeaweedFS S3)
release_note:
- First version. Same Ente stack as the MinIO build, with SeaweedFS 4.22 in place of MinIO.
- SeaweedFS is pinned to a real version tag. The Ente server and web images only publish floating tags, so there is no single version field to track for the app as a whole.
- s3.json is written by a busybox init service instead of being bind-mounted as a file, because a missing file on the host becomes an empty directory and breaks the container in a confusing way.
- master.volumeSizeLimitMB is set to 1024 so three buckets do not reserve far more disk than a home NAS has.
- No socat sidecar. The S3 endpoint is the box's own IP, which both the server and phones can reach.
- No storage-unlimited container. It ran a full extra Postgres image forever just to poll one column. Raising storage is now a one-time docker exec command in the install tips.
